approved: Proceeds of Crime Amendment (Proceeds and Other Matters) Bill 2017

The Proceeds of Crime Amendment (Proceeds and Other Matters) Bill 2017 amends the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 to allow authorities to restrain and forfeit property where illicit funds are used for mortgage repayments or improvements, closing a loophole that enabled organised crime to avoid forfeiture.

Labor supported the Proceeds of Crime Amendment (Proceeds and Other Matters) Bill 2017, which makes technical amendments to close loopholes identified in the Huang and Hart cases, clarifying that property can be considered proceeds of crime if crime money is used to pay off mortgages or improve it. The speaker also criticised the government for cutting $184 million from the Australian Federal Police and losing 151 personnel.

The speaker supported the Proceeds of Crime Amendment (Proceeds and Other Matters) Bill 2017, arguing it closes a loophole where courts (in Commissioner of the Australian Federal Police v Huang and v Hart) ruled that proceeds of crime cannot be traced beyond the initial purchase. He emphasised the need to attack criminal business models by following the money, citing that serious and organised crime costs Australia $36 billion a year.

The speaker supported the Proceeds of Crime Amendment (Proceeds and Other Matters) Bill 2017, which tightens loopholes in unexplained wealth and proceeds of crime laws. He also raised concerns about illegal tobacco due to high taxation creating a $1.67 to $40 price gap, and car theft, noting up to 40% of stolen cars are exported, urging stronger export regulations.

The speaker supported the Proceeds of Crime Amendment Bill 2017 but argued it may create new loopholes while noting the government cut $184 million from the Australian Federal Police budget in 2017-18, leading to 151 officers being let go. They also pointed out the amendments respond to the 2016 *Commissioner of the Australian Federal Police v Huang* case, which could have been resolved via a pecuniary penalty order instead of legislative change.

The speaker supported the Proceeds of Crime Amendment Bill 2017 to close loopholes exposed in the Huang and Hart cases, but criticised the government for cutting $184 million from the Australian Federal Police and reducing AFP personnel in Tasmania from 30 to five, while announcing Labor's commitment to restore a permanent AFP presence at Hobart airport with 21 officers.
Proceeds of Crime Amendment (Proceeds and Other Matters) Act 2018
